title: The creatinine after the new antibiotic
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; they are not targets. No doses are given. Your hospital’s protocol and the attending nephrologist decide every order.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on the renal rotation of a provincial hospital in Batangas. Mrs. Teresita Villanueva, 62, a retired market vendor, was admitted six days ago with community-acquired pneumonia and started on an intravenous penicillin. Her cough and fever have improved. Her creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL on admission.

At 07:30 on day 6 the intern, Dr. Paolo Reyes, calls you. This morning’s creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL. She has a low-grade temperature and a fine rash on her trunk that the nurses noticed yesterday. Her urine output is still adequate. This module calls the likely problem acute interstitial nephritis (AIN): an immune reaction in the tissue around the tubules, most often caused by a drug.

n1.prompt: What do you ask Dr. Reyes to do first?

choices.text: Hold anything obviously nephrotoxic and recheck the creatinine tomorrow morning.
choices.feedback: Holding nephrotoxins is sensible, but without a dated list you do not know which drug started the reaction or when. Tomorrow’s creatinine will not tell you the cause.
choices.then: You call back and ask for the dated drug list and the sediment. Within the hour, Dr. Reyes reports: the penicillin and omeprazole were started on admission, and her daughter says she has taken mefenamic acid from the sari-sari store for knee pain for three weeks. The sediment shows white cells and white cell casts, with no bacteria.

vitals.sed: White cells, white cell casts, no bacteria

choices.text: List every drug started in the past month and examine the urine sediment yourselves.
choices.feedback: Drug-induced disease is thought to underlie 60% to 70% of AIN, so the dated timeline is the main diagnostic tool. The sediment shows whether the interstitium is inflamed: sterile pyuria and white cell casts. Include over-the-counter and herbal products, with dates.
choices.then: Within the hour, Dr. Reyes reports: the penicillin and omeprazole were started on admission, and her daughter says she has taken mefenamic acid from the sari-sari store for knee pain for three weeks. The sediment shows white cells and white cell casts, with no bacteria.

vitals.sed: White cells, white cell casts, no bacteria

choices.text: Send urine for eosinophils and wait for the result before changing anything.
choices.feedback: Urine eosinophils have limited diagnostic value, so a positive or negative result will not settle the question. Waiting delays the one step that matters most: stopping the culprit drug.
choices.then: You ask for the dated drug list and the sediment instead. Dr. Reyes reports: the penicillin and omeprazole were started on admission, and she has taken mefenamic acid from the sari-sari store for three weeks. The sediment shows white cells and white cell casts, with no bacteria.

vitals.sed: White cells, white cell casts, no bacteria

choices.text: Treat the pyuria as a new urinary infection and add a second antibiotic.
choices.feedback: White cells with no bacteria and white cell casts point to interstitial inflammation, not infection. A second antibiotic adds another possible culprit.
choices.then: You cancel the order and ask for the dated drug list and the sediment. Dr. Reyes reports: the penicillin and omeprazole were started on admission, and she has taken mefenamic acid for three weeks. The sediment shows white cells and white cell casts, with no bacteria.

vitals.sed: White cells, white cell casts, no bacteria

n2.prompt: Her pneumonia still needs treatment. What do you do with her medicines?

choices.text: Keep everything. The pneumonia needs the penicillin and her knees need the mefenamic acid. Recheck in a week.
choices.feedback: Stopping the culprit drug promptly is the mainstay of treatment. Every day the trigger continues, the inflammation can move toward permanent fibrosis.
choices.then: The attending reviews the chart at noon and asks you to stop the suspect drugs today. The penicillin is replaced, the mefenamic acid and omeprazole are stopped.

choices.text: Stop the mefenamic acid, since NSAIDs are a known cause, and keep the penicillin for the pneumonia.
choices.feedback: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are a known cause, but penicillins are too, and the timing fits the penicillin well. Leaving one likely trigger running keeps the reaction going.
choices.then: On review with the attending, the penicillin is replaced as well, and the omeprazole is stopped because she has no firm reason to take it.

choices.text: Stop all three suspect drugs and ask the attending for an antibiotic from another class.
choices.feedback: Penicillins, NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors are all usual culprits, and all three fit the timeline. Stopping them early is the step most likely to save kidney function, while the pneumonia is still treated with a different class. Stop the penicillin, the mefenamic acid and the omeprazole; trend creatinine daily.

n3.scene: Three days after the drugs were stopped, her creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL and still rising. Her rash is fading. Urine output is still adequate.

choices.text: Start a glucocorticoid yourself tonight, since the module says early is better.
choices.feedback: Timing matters, but steroids, and the biopsy that often comes first, are a decision the fellow and attending make together. A presumptive diagnosis is not acceptable when steroids are being considered.
choices.then: The nurse asks you to confirm the order with the attending. You call; the attending asks you to hold it and plans to see her today.

vitals.plan: Attending review today: biopsy and steroids

choices.text: Call the attending today: rising creatinine after stopping the drugs.
choices.feedback: A presumptive diagnosis is acceptable only when creatinine falls within days of stopping the drug. A definitive diagnosis needs a biopsy, and in the Madrid series a delay of weeks before steroids was associated with incomplete recovery and more fibrosis. Biopsy and steroids need deciding within days.

vitals.plan: Attending review today: biopsy and steroids

choices.text: Order a gallium scan and repeat urine eosinophils to confirm AIN before calling anyone.
choices.feedback: Both tests have limited utility, and neither replaces a biopsy. Ordering them costs days that this patient may not have.
choices.then: The fellow sees the order and calls the attending, who plans to see her today.

vitals.plan: Attending review today: biopsy and steroids

choices.text: Give it three more weeks. AIN often recovers once the drug is out.
choices.feedback: Recovery within days is reassuring; a creatinine still climbing on day 3 is not. In the Madrid series, patients whose steroids were delayed by about a month did not return to baseline, and repeat biopsies showed more fibrosis.
choices.then: The fellow reviews the trend that afternoon and calls the attending, who plans to see her today.

vitals.plan: Attending review today: biopsy and steroids

n4.scene: The biopsy shows an interstitial infiltrate with eosinophils and tubulitis, and only mild fibrosis. The attending plans to start a glucocorticoid. Her son, a jeepney driver, asks you: “Will the steroid cure her kidneys?”

choices.text: “Stopping the drugs was the main treatment. Steroids may help most when started early.”
choices.feedback: The evidence is observational: a retrospective review of 61 patients, open to confounding. It supports deciding early but does not prove benefit, and the family deserves that honesty. The studies are not proof; they suggest recovery is better when steroids start early, which is why we are starting now.

choices.text: “Yes. Steroids are proven to bring the kidneys back to normal in this condition.”
choices.feedback: No trial has proven this. The evidence is a retrospective series and expert review, which call the benefit unproven though apparently positive when started early.

choices.text: “Let us wait and see how she responds; it is too early to say anything definite.”
choices.feedback: True as far as it goes, but it leaves him without the one thing he can understand: why the steroid is given and what the evidence does and does not show.

n5.scene: A week later her creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL and falling. She is going home with a follow-up in the renal clinic.
n5.prompt: What must happen before she leaves?

choices.text: Write “drug-induced AIN” in the discharge summary so the next doctor knows.
choices.feedback: The diagnosis belongs in the summary, but a summary is not read at the next pharmacy counter or the next admission. The suspect drugs must be listed as allergies in the chart, and she must know them by name.

choices.text: Tell her she can restart mefenamic acid for her knees once her creatinine is normal.
choices.feedback: Re-exposure to the culprit can trigger the reaction again. NSAIDs are best avoided in anyone who has had kidney injury from them.

choices.text: Record both culprits under allergies and tell them by name, in Tagalog, to avoid them.
choices.feedback: Writing the culprit as an allergy is the fellow’s job in the module, so it is never restarted. In the Philippines, NSAIDs are sold without prescription, so she must recognize the names herself. The penicillin and mefenamic acid as suspected culprits; avoid other NSAIDs from the store.

end.title: Clinic, six weeks later
end.text: Her creatinine has settled at 1.2 mg/dL, a little above her admission value. The glucocorticoid is being tapered by the attending. She carries a card listing the penicillin and mefenamic acid, and her son has thrown out the tablets at home.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • The dated drug list is the diagnostic test. Include over-the-counter and herbal products; drugs are thought to underlie 60% to 70% of AIN.
  • Stop every likely culprit first, and treat the underlying infection with a different class.
  • A creatinine still rising days after stopping the drug means calling the attending to decide on biopsy and steroids within days, not weeks; fibrosis does not wait.
  • Say how strong the evidence is: steroids for AIN rest on observational data that favor an early start but do not prove benefit.
  • Write the culprit as an allergy and teach the patient its name.

See Interstitial nephritis.
